title: Dilmun
subtitle: c.3000–1200 BC · The Bronze Age Entrepôt of the Gulf — Bahrain, Tarut and Failaka

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: From the cuneiform frontier to a Kassite Babylonian province

entries.label: Dilmun enters the cuneiform record
entries.loc: Referenced from Uruk, Lagash and Ur (S. Iraq); homeland Bahrain–Eastern Arabia
entries.hint: Dilmun appears in the earliest administrative tablets of Uruk and in the inscriptions of Ur-Nanshe of Lagash, who records ships of Dilmun bringing timber. From its first documentation Dilmun is defined by what it ships north, not by its kings.
entries.note: Archaic Uruk texts (sign DILMUN on a taxation tablet); Ur-Nanshe of Lagash foundation inscriptions, c.2500 BC (Frayne, RIME 1). Discussed in Crawford, 'Dilmun and its Gulf Neighbours' (1998).

entries.label: Sargon of Akkad — 'ships of Dilmun, Magan and Meluhha'
entries.hint: Sargon of Akkad boasts that ships from Dilmun, Magan and Meluhha moored at the quay of his capital. The formula fixes Dilmun as the nearest of the three Gulf trading lands and the gateway to the others.
entries.note: Sargon of Akkad inscription, 'the ships of Meluhha, Magan and Dilmun he made moor at the quay of Agade' (Frayne, RIME 2.1.1). c.2334–2279 BC.

entries.label: The walled capital at Qal'at al-Bahrain
entries.loc: Qal'at al-Bahrain (City II), north coast of Bahrain
entries.hint: Dilmun's peak: a fortified town of some 15 hectares at Qal'at al-Bahrain with a city wall, planned streets, warehouses and a temple, running the transit trade between Mesopotamia and the lands to the east. This is the Dilmun of the Ur merchant archives.
entries.note: Danish expedition (Bibby & Glob) 1954–65; French mission (Pierre Lombard, Monik Kervran) from 1977. Højlund & Andersen, 'Qala'at al-Bahrain' vol. 1 (1994).

entries.label: Uballissu-Marduk — Kassite governor of Dilmun
entries.hint: A cache of clay tablets from Qal'at al-Bahrain names Uballissu-Marduk, governor of Dilmun under the Kassite kings of Babylon, writing to subordinates about dates, taxes and personnel. Dilmun has become a Babylonian province run by an appointed official.
entries.note: Qal'at al-Bahrain Kassite tablet archive; edition by Kh. Nashef, 'The Deities of Dilmun' and the governor letters (BBVO). c.14th century BC.

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: A trading state that armed its warehouses — the militarised Gulf of the Bronze Age

entries.label: Naram-Sin's fleet and the Gulf as a war theatre
entries.hint: Naram-Sin of Akkad campaigned by sea against Magan and claims to have crossed 'the Lower Sea' with ships. Dilmun, the hinge of that sea, first appears in the record inside a world in which the dominant Mesopotamian power now projected armed force down the Gulf.
entries.note: Naram-Sin inscriptions on the Magan campaign (Frayne, RIME 2.1.4); discussed in Potts, 'The Arabian Gulf in Antiquity' vol. 1 (1990), ch. 4.

entries.label: The fortification of the entrepôt
entries.hint: City II was given a stone-founded wall with towers and gates — the first monumental fortification in the Gulf. An unwalled Neolithic coast had become a place where the warehouses on which the whole transit trade depended needed defending against raiding and piracy.
entries.note: Højlund & Andersen, 'Qala'at al-Bahrain' vol. 1 (1994), the City II wall sequence; the interpretation of the wall as a response to maritime insecurity is standard.

entries.label: The Sealand kings and the head of the Gulf
entries.loc: Southern Mesopotamian marshes; the Gulf head
entries.hint: After the fall of Hammurabi's dynasty the First Sealand Dynasty held the marshland approaches to the Gulf, controlling — and disrupting — the sea route between Babylonia and Dilmun. One Sealand king even bears a name compounded with the Dilmun god Inzak.
entries.note: The First Sealand Dynasty king-list and the Tell Khaiber archive (Dalley, 'Babylonian Tablets from the First Sealand Dynasty', 2009); the Dilmun connection in Potts (1990) vol. 1, ch. 6.

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: Weights, seals and the machinery of a mercantile state

entries.label: The Dilmun weight standard
entries.loc: Bahrain; matched at Ur, Susa and Lothal
entries.hint: Dilmun regulated Gulf trade with a standardised weight of about 13.4 grams and its multiples. Balance weights on this standard turn up from southern Mesopotamia to the Indus port of Lothal — a shared commercial measure Dilmun helped enforce.
entries.note: L. Hemmy's early analysis; G. Weisgerber and others on the 'Dilmun standard'; Roaf & Galbraith on Gulf weights. Lothal parallels: S.R. Rao's excavation reports.

entries.label: The Dilmun stamp seal as a legal instrument
entries.hint: Round stamp seals in a distinctive local style were used to seal jars, doors and clay tags, authenticating transactions. Their sudden appearance in quantity marks the moment Dilmun's trade became bureaucratised.
entries.note: P. Kjærum, 'The Stamp and Cylinder Seals' (Failaka/Dilmun vol. 1.1, 1983); Al-Sindi, 'Dilmun Seals' (Bahrain National Museum).

entries.label: The Kassite governor's archive
entries.hint: The Kassite-period tablets from Qal'at al-Bahrain record ration lists, date-palm accounting and the movement of workers — the paperwork of a provincial administration reporting to Babylon. Dilmun is now governed, not merely traded with.
entries.note: Kh. Nashef and the Bahrain Kassite tablets; see also Højlund & Andersen, 'Qala'at al-Bahrain' vol. 2 (1997).

entries.label: Temple estates and offerings at Barbar
entries.hint: The Barbar temple complex controlled land, livestock and a sacred spring, receiving offerings recorded on sealed tags. In Dilmun as in Mesopotamia, the temple was an economic institution as much as a religious one.
entries.note: H.H. Andersen & F. Højlund, 'The Barbar Temples' (2003); Danish excavations 1954–61.

entries.label: Failaka as Dilmun's northern administrative outpost
entries.hint: Failaka, at the head of the Gulf, held a fortified settlement with its own temple and hundreds of seals — an extension of the Dilmun administrative system placed to watch the approaches from Mesopotamia.
entries.note: Danish and later French/Kuwaiti excavations on Failaka; F. Højlund, 'The Bronze Age Pottery' (Failaka vol. 2, 1987).

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: Inzak of Agarum, the water temple at Barbar, and Dilmun the paradise

entries.label: Inzak and Meskilak — the gods of Dilmun
entries.hint: Dilmun's chief god was Inzak, 'lord of Agarum', paired with the goddess Meskilak. Their names recur on seals and dedications from Bahrain to Failaka, and Mesopotamian god-lists slot Inzak in beside their own deities.
entries.note: Kh. Nashef, 'The Deities of Dilmun', in 'Bahrain through the Ages' (1986); Inzak in the Mesopotamian god-list An = Anum.

entries.label: The Barbar water temple
entries.hint: Three temples were built one above another at Barbar around a stepped stone basin fed by a spring — a shrine to the sweet water that made Bahrain habitable. A copper bull's head and votive figures were found in its precinct.
entries.note: H.H. Andersen & F. Højlund, 'The Barbar Temples' (2003). The copper bull's head is in the Bahrain National Museum.

entries.label: Serpent burials and ritual deposits
entries.hint: Bowls containing the bones of sea snakes, sometimes with a bead, were buried in the foundations of buildings at Qal'at al-Bahrain and in the Failaka temple. The practice links Dilmun ritual to the sea and the underworld.
entries.note: Danish excavation records; the snake-bowl deposits discussed by Bibby, 'Looking for Dilmun' (1969) and later by Lombard.

entries.label: Dilmun as the pure land in Sumerian myth
entries.loc: Nippur and Ur (tablet findspots); the myth set in Dilmun
entries.hint: In 'Enki and Ninhursag', Dilmun is a land 'pure, clean and bright' where no illness or death exists — until Enki disrupts it. Elsewhere the flood survivor Ziusudra is settled in Dilmun 'where the sun rises'. Mesopotamia imagined Dilmun as a paradise at the edge of the world.
entries.note: 'Enki and Ninhursag' (ETCSL 1.1.1); the Sumerian Flood Story / 'Eridu Genesis' on Ziusudra in Dilmun. Old Babylonian copies.

entries.label: The burial-mound landscape as an afterlife geography
entries.loc: A'ali, Saar, Hamad Town mound-fields, Bahrain
entries.hint: Tens of thousands of low earth-and-stone mounds cover central Bahrain, each over a single chambered grave with a few pots, a seal and personal ornaments. The scale of the cemetery suggests a society that invested heavily in provisioning its dead.
entries.note: Recent reassessment: the mounds are a normal-population cemetery, not elite-only — S.F. Andersen & the Bahrain Burial Mounds project; UNESCO World Heritage inscription (2019).

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: The Dilmun seal, the great mounds of A'ali and Barbar ridged ware

entries.label: The Dilmun stamp-seal style
entries.hint: Dilmun seals are round, high-backed and cut with gazelles, seated figures drinking through straws, bull-men and stars — a coherent local iconography distinct from Mesopotamian and Indus glyptic. They are Dilmun's signature art form.
entries.note: P. Kjærum, 'The Stamp and Cylinder Seals' (1983); H. Al-Sindi, 'Dilmun Seals' (1999). Over 600 recorded.

entries.label: The Royal Mounds of A'ali
entries.hint: A cluster of two-storey stone-chambered tumuli up to 15 metres high and 45 across stands apart from the ordinary mound-fields. These are Dilmun's monumental tombs — the clearest sign of an emerging ruling class.
entries.note: Excavated by the Danish expedition and later the Bahrain authorities; part of the 'Dilmun Burial Mounds' UNESCO World Heritage property (2019).

entries.label: The copper bull's head of Barbar
entries.loc: Barbar Temple, Bahrain (now Bahrain National Museum)
entries.hint: A hollow-cast copper head of a bull, once mounted on a lyre in the Mesopotamian manner, was found in the Barbar precinct. It is the finest surviving Dilmun metalwork and shows craftsmen working to a high Near Eastern standard.
entries.note: Danish excavation of Barbar Temple II; Andersen & Højlund (2003). Compare the bull-lyres of Ur.

entries.label: Barbar red ridged ware
entries.hint: Dilmun's characteristic pottery — thin, ring-based jars with a red slip and a rilled or ridged shoulder — was made in quantity on Bahrain and exported around the Gulf, a recognisable Dilmun brand in the archaeological record.
entries.note: F. Højlund, 'The Bronze Age Pottery' (Failaka vol. 2, 1987); the 'Barbar ware' / 'chain-ridge ware' type series.

entries.label: The straw-drinking banquet on Dilmun seals
entries.hint: A recurring seal scene shows two seated figures drinking from a large jar through long straws, sometimes flanking a standard or an animal. The motif — shared with Mesopotamia — depicts a ritual feast, the nearest thing to a performance record Dilmun has left.
entries.note: Kjærum (1983) seal catalogue, the 'drinking scene' class; compare Early Dynastic Mesopotamian banquet plaques.

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: Cuneiform on Bahrain, metrology, and Dilmun in the Mesopotamian map of the world

entries.label: Scribes and cuneiform literacy at Qal'at al-Bahrain
entries.hint: The Kassite-period tablets prove trained scribes were working on Bahrain, writing Akkadian in the Babylonian manner. Dilmun was inside the cuneiform world, not merely visited by it.
entries.note: Bahrain Kassite tablet archive (Nashef); palaeography consistent with mainstream Middle Babylonian scribal training.

entries.label: Weight-based reckoning across three trade systems
entries.hint: Dilmun merchants worked fluently between the Mesopotamian shekel, their own ~13.4 g standard and Indus binary weights, converting values across all three. This applied arithmetic of exchange was Dilmun's core professional knowledge.
entries.note: Analyses of Gulf weight assemblages (Roaf; De Jesus); the interoperability of the Dilmun, Mesopotamian and Harappan systems.

entries.label: 'Where the sun rises' — Dilmun in Mesopotamian cosmography
entries.hint: Mesopotamian texts place Dilmun at the sunrise edge of the inhabited world, the last land before the cosmic sea. It was a real place doing real trade, but it also marked the boundary of the Mesopotamian mental map.
entries.note: Dilmun in the Sumerian Flood Story, 'Enki and Ninhursag', and the Babylonian Map of the World tradition (BM 92687 names nearby regions). Horowitz, 'Mesopotamian Cosmic Geography' (1998).

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: The Gulf's indispensable middleman — copper, dates and the trade of Ur

entries.label: Dilmun the entrepôt
entries.hint: Mesopotamian barley, wool, textiles, sesame oil and silver came south to Dilmun and were exchanged for copper from Magan and carnelian, ivory, timber and gold from Meluhha. Dilmun produced little of this itself; it took a cut on all of it.
entries.note: Reconstructed from the Ur III and Old Babylonian 'Dilmun trade' texts; W.F. Leemans, 'Foreign Trade in the Old Babylonian Period' (1960).

entries.label: The alik Tilmun merchants of Ur and Ea-nasir
entries.hint: At Ur, associations of 'those who go to Dilmun' financed copper voyages, pooling temple silver and private capital. One of them, Ea-nasir, is immortalised in a customer's clay tablet complaining that the copper he delivered was sub-standard and his manner rude.
entries.note: The Ea-nasir archive from Ur, including UET V 81 (the Nanni complaint tablet, British Museum). A.L. Oppenheim, 'The Seafaring Merchants of Ur', JAOS 74 (1954).

entries.label: Magan copper re-exported through Dilmun
entries.hint: Copper was the trade's backbone. Oman's ore reached Mesopotamia via Dilmun by the tonne — one Ur text logs over 18 tonnes in a single consignment — until Old Babylonian buyers began dealing with Magan directly.
entries.note: Ur III copper-import texts (Leemans 1960); Weisgerber's fieldwork on Omani copper (Maysar, 'Ancient Copper Production in Oman').

entries.label: The date gardens of Bahrain
entries.hint: Artesian springs let Bahrain grow dense date palm groves and cereals under them — the agricultural base that fed the towns and supplied dates as a trade good. Kassite accounts tax this palm cultivation directly.
entries.note: Kassite governor tablets on date accounting (Nashef); Bahrain's spring-fed agriculture described by later Greek visitors (Theophrastus on Tylos).

entries.label: The entrepôt collapses, c.1700 BC
entries.hint: When Indus trade withered and Old Babylonian merchants bypassed Bahrain for direct Magan dealings, Dilmun's transit economy fell away. Qal'at al-Bahrain shrank; the great mound-building slowed. Dilmun continued, smaller, as a Kassite dependency.
entries.note: Højlund on the City II–III transition at Qal'at al-Bahrain; the mid-2nd-millennium contraction across the Gulf trade network (Potts 1990, vol. 1).

categories.label: Technology
categories.subtitle: Tapping the aquifer, building the mounds and the seagoing plank boat

entries.label: Artesian well engineering
entries.loc: Barbar, A'ali and the Bahrain mound-fields
entries.hint: Dilmun builders sank stone-lined shafts to tap the artesian aquifer, most spectacularly the stepped water basin under the Barbar temple. Control of sweet water — including famous springs bubbling up offshore — underpinned everything else.
entries.note: Barbar temple water installation (Andersen & Højlund 2003); the offshore freshwater springs noted from antiquity to the 20th century.

entries.label: Chambered burial-mound construction
entries.hint: The larger Dilmun tombs use dressed stone chambers with corbelled or capstone roofs, ringwalls and, in the A'ali 'royal' mounds, two storeys — a repeatable engineering solution scaled up for elite burials.
entries.note: Danish and Bahraini excavation of the A'ali mounds; construction analysis in the 'Dilmun Burial Mounds' UNESCO dossier (2019).

entries.label: Seagoing plank boats and the magilum-boat
entries.loc: Gulf shipping lanes; depicted on seals
entries.hint: Mesopotamian texts distinguish the large 'Magan-boat' and 'Dilmun-boat' from river craft. Reed hulls gave way to bitumen-sealed sewn-plank vessels able to carry tonnes of copper across open water in the summer sailing season.
entries.note: Ship terminology in the Ur III texts (Potts 1995, 'Distant Shores'); bitumen-with-barnacles boat fragments from Gulf sites (Carter 2006 for the technique's antiquity).

entries.label: The city wall of Qal'at al-Bahrain
entries.hint: City II was enclosed by a substantial stone-founded wall with towers and gates — the first monumental fortification in the Gulf, protecting the warehouses on which the whole trade depended.
entries.note: Højlund & Andersen, 'Qala'at al-Bahrain' vol. 1 (1994), the City II wall sequence.

entries.label: Copper working on Bahrain
entries.hint: Crucibles, moulds and slag show Dilmun smiths casting tools, weapons and fine objects like the Barbar bull from imported copper, adding tin for bronze. Dilmun did not mine metal but it finished it.
entries.note: Metallurgical debris from Qal'at al-Bahrain and the Saar settlement (Killick & Moon, 'The Early Dilmun Settlement at Saar', 2005).

categories.label: Exchange
categories.subtitle: Dilmun–Magan–Meluhha: the Gulf as the highway between Mesopotamia and the Indus

entries.label: The Dilmun–Magan–Meluhha triangle
entries.hint: Akkadian royal inscriptions name Dilmun, Magan and Meluhha together as the three lands reached by sea. Dilmun was the hinge: goods from the Indus (Meluhha) and Oman (Magan) passed through Bahrain on their way to Mesopotamia and back.
entries.note: Sargon of Akkad and Gudea of Lagash inscriptions (Frayne, RIME 2–3); synthesis in Potts, 'The Arabian Gulf in Antiquity' vol. 1 (1990).

entries.label: Indus goods and weights at Dilmun
entries.hint: Etched carnelian beads, ivory, Indus-standard cubical weights and a handful of Indus-inscribed seals at Bahrain and Failaka show direct contact with Harappan ports. Dilmun sat where the Indus and Mesopotamian worlds physically met.
entries.note: Indus weights and etched carnelian from Qal'at al-Bahrain and Failaka; the 'Persian Gulf' hybrid seal type (Kjærum 1983). Meluhhan traders at Lagash: the 'Meluhha village' texts.

entries.label: The 'Gulf seal' as a shared trade script
entries.loc: Failaka, Bahrain, Tarut; a specimen at Lothal (Gujarat)
entries.hint: Before the fully local Dilmun style crystallised, a round 'Persian Gulf' seal type — Mesopotamian technique, mixed motifs — circulated among Gulf and Indus merchants. One turned up at the Harappan port of Lothal, marking the network's far end.
entries.note: Kjærum, 'Seals of a Persian Gulf type' (1980s); the Lothal 'Persian Gulf' seal published by S.R. Rao.

entries.label: Tarut and the eastern Arabian mainland in the Dilmun world
entries.loc: Tarut island and Qatif oasis, eastern Arabia
entries.hint: Tarut island off Qatif produced Early Dynastic-style statuary, chlorite vessels and rich graves — a mainland partner (perhaps the original core) of the Dilmun polity before Bahrain became dominant. The 'land of Dilmun' straddled the water.
entries.note: The Tarut statue and 'intercultural style' chlorite vessels; A. Masry, 'Prehistory in Northeastern Arabia' (1974); Potts (1990) vol. 1.

categories.label: World
categories.subtitle: The Akkadian naming, the Indus decline and the Kassite settlement

entries.label: The Akkadian Empire names the Gulf lands
entries.hint: Sargon and his successors, projecting power to the sea, fixed 'Dilmun', 'Magan' and 'Meluhha' in the written record for the first time. The Gulf entered history as the maritime frontier of the world's first empire.
entries.note: Old Akkadian royal inscriptions (Frayne, RIME 2); Naram-Sin's campaign to Magan.

entries.label: The decline of the Indus Civilisation
entries.hint: As Harappan cities were abandoned and the integrated Indus system unravelled, the Meluhha trade that fed Dilmun's entrepôt dried up. The event that ended one civilisation hollowed out the economy of another a thousand miles away.
entries.note: Standard Indus chronology (Kenoyer; Possehl, 'The Indus Civilization', 2002); the coincident Gulf trade contraction (Potts 1990).

entries.label: Kassite Babylon absorbs Dilmun
entries.hint: Under the Kassite dynasty, Babylon extended formal control over Dilmun, installing a governor and provisioning the island from the mainland. Dilmun spent the later Bronze Age as the seaward province of a Mesopotamian kingdom.
entries.note: Kassite governor archive at Qal'at al-Bahrain; Kassite administrative reach discussed in Potts (1990) vol. 1, ch. 7.

categories.label: Lives
categories.subtitle: Who lies under the mounds — an ordinary population, its women, and an emerging elite

entries.label: The mounds are everyone's graves
entries.hint: Long read as the tombs of a privileged class, the Dilmun mounds are now understood as the cemetery of the whole population: men, women, infants, each in a single-chamber grave with a pot and a personal item. Monumental burial was a norm, not a privilege.
entries.note: S.F. Andersen and the Bahrain Burial Mounds project reassessment; UNESCO 'Dilmun Burial Mounds' inscription (2019) states the majority are ordinary graves.

entries.label: Women buried with seals and ornament
entries.hint: A number of women's graves contain stamp seals — the instruments of commercial and legal life — alongside beads of gold, carnelian and shell. It suggests women in Dilmun could hold property and transact in their own right.
entries.note: Grave-good associations from the Saar cemetery (Killick & Moon 2005) and the A'ali mounds; seals in female burials noted by Al-Sindi.

entries.label: Infant jar-burials under the house floor at Saar
entries.hint: At the Saar village, dead infants were placed in pottery jars and buried beneath the floors of houses rather than in the mound cemetery — keeping the youngest dead within the household. Different rites marked different stages of belonging.
entries.note: London-Bahrain Archaeological Expedition, 'The Early Dilmun Settlement at Saar' (Killick & Moon, 2005), infant burials.

entries.label: A date-heavy diet written in Dilmun teeth
entries.hint: Skeletons from the mounds show heavy tooth wear and high rates of caries — the signature of a diet built on dates and other sugars, supplemented by fish. The trade wealth of Dilmun did not translate into robust health for most of its people.
entries.note: Palaeodietary and dental studies of the Bahrain mound populations (e.g. Littleton & Frohlich, 'Fish-eaters and farmers: dental pathology in the Arabian Gulf', AJPA 101, 1996).
